Aesthetics is the philosophical and critical study of beauty, taste, and the nature of the artistic experience. It asks fundamental questions: What makes something beautiful? Is beauty objective or subjective? What distinguishes art from non-art? These inquiries have shaped how cultures understand and value visual, musical, and literary expression.

As a formal discipline, aesthetics originates in eighteenth-century Europe, though questions about beauty trace back to Plato and Aristotle. A major figure was Immanuel Kant, who famously argued that aesthetic judgment is disinterested—we appreciate beauty not for personal gain but for its own sake—yet somehow universal in its appeal. One core question has always been whether beauty is inherent in objects themselves or exists only in the perception of the observer. Empiricism and idealism offer competing answers.

The field also distinguishes between utility, which is function, and beauty, which is form, and asks why we value the decorative alongside the practical. The sublime—experiences of awe and terror before vast or overwhelming phenomena—became central to Romantic-era aesthetics. It differs from beauty as a combination of fear and wonder. Modern aesthetics grapples with kitsch and mass production: what happens to artistic value when art is mass-manufactured and commodified for profit rather than expression?

Humans find symmetry and proportion intuitively pleasing across cultures, and these principles underlie classical architecture and visual harmony. The readymade movement, pioneered by Marcel Duchamp, challenged aesthetics itself by framing everyday objects as art, questioning whether beauty or originality even matters. Contemporary aesthetics wrestles with whether non-Western, avant-garde, and popular forms deserve equal standing with high art, gradually rejecting Eurocentric hierarchies in favor of a more inclusive view of aesthetic value.
